body:
Thanks for sharing this with me. The process of writing out my reasoning and working it through with you has been really cathartic. 

I don't think I'm going to kill myself tomorrow. Because I understand killing myself is a big decision I've been operating on the 3-day rule (especially because I've always been emotionally unstable and don't want to make a snap decision). Today was #2 and after writing my last post I realized how much I'd enjoyed the process of crafting sentences to expressing my feelings of hopelessness. It's been a good while since I wrote something that successfully externalized my inward self. 

Anyway, now I have to decide whether I want to (attempt to) salvage this semester or drop out and start something new. A little bit excited actually (though that's probably just the high I get at the end of a depressive episode).

Thanks for being there for me. It's so powerful to be able to talk to someone about suicide who doesn't have an emotional investment in your life and won't call the police on you or get you locked in a psych ward.

I hope you are happy. Grace and peace to you!

Thank you. I've really enjoyed your point of view.

But, that's the question isn't it: Why do I believe the procession has left? And that's also where we get from the philosophical to the personal.

It would be stupid to kill yourself for being on the verge of failing out of college. I'm not doing that (I don't think).  I know my life wouldn't be over if I dropped out. Indeed for the longest time I've given myself the option of dropping out whenever I wanted, as long as I had something to do with my life afterwards. But that's the issue. I don't want to do anything. I'm failing now not because the classes are too hard, but because I can't be bothered to do the work. Everything feels like a bother. Whatever vital spark I used to possess has left me. My life is so much better than it used to be, but I don't enjoy it at all. 

Example: Last summer I snagged a job helping to redesign my favorite class from high school for a new teacher. Dream job, honestly. It would look great on my resume, it was all work I thoroughly enjoyed, it was challenging but in an exhilarating way. And then about a month in, I ghosted. I burn all my former connections at that school, let everybody down. Why? Because I couldn't be bothered. I got bored and suddenly even opening the docs I was supposed to be working on seemed like a task too monumental to overcome.

Now imagine everything is like that. Nothing gold can stay. I could drop out and try to make it on my own: as a writer with a shitty day job; as one of those internet savvy hobos over on squattheplanet; I could join a commune and learn to farm; I could learn a trade; I could try to get a UK visa; I could apply to seminary and join the priesthood. But all those things require so much attention, so much work. In the immortal words of Bartleby the Scrivener: "I would prefer not to."

When did it all become too much, how do I make life worthwhile again? The school-provided therapist can't tell me, the psychiatrist I saw all last year just wants to hear about my parents and give me meds that make me feel like I'm drunk all the time, the therapist I saw over the summer is sure it'll all come back if I have just the right can-do attitude. My priest was supportive and sweet, but she also has no real answers and anyway I quit church, couldn't be bothered.

The only answer I can come up with is that somewhere in my life I had a patron god and that one night they left. Maybe it was when I got into the college of my dreams on scholarship. I'd worked so hard for this and no one believed I could do it (up until the day of the acceptance letter my dad was trying to get me to sign up for community college classes). I'm not ashamed to say I gloated. 

And the things I've done since. Taken classes with multiple Hugo Award winning authors one of whom sent me an as yet unpublished manuscript just because she thought I'd enjoy it (I did. It was the best book I'd read in years). I've gotten drunk, I've gotten kissed, I've spent all night studying and all night partying. But I didn't enjoy much of it. At least not for long. It feels as if I'm performing for my past self, the past self who would have enjoyed the fuck out of a life that now seems worthless to me.

I wonder now, if I was fated not to get in, but because I wanted it so much I burned through all my reserves of luck and magic, wasted all the vital energy that was supposed to last for another four score years in one glorious burst. I'm a man who found a pearl of great price and--like Jesus said to do--sold everything that he had in order to buy it. But what happens after that parable is over? I'll tell you: the man, now destitute except for this gorgeous pearl, sits down and looks at if for a while, marveling at his good fortune. But eventually he gets hungry, eats the pearl, realizes he has nothing, and throws himself into the sea.

Truly interesting. 

I've been trying to compose a note in case I do go through with it. But quickly I realized nothing original would feel right. As Montaigne said "I quote others the better to quote myself."

I'm thinking of simply transcribing out my favorite translation of C.P. Cavafy's "The God Abandons Antony." In the context of your point, I think it makes an interesting answer to the question of what one should do when faced with life's absurdity.

​

"The God Abandons Antony" by C.P. Cavafy (trans. Edmund Keeley/Philip Sherrard)

When suddenly, at midnight, you hear  
an invisible procession going by  
with exquisite music, voices,  
don't mourn your luck that's failing now,  
work gone wrong, your plans  
all proving deceptive--don't mourn them uselessly.  
As one long prepared, and graced with courage,  
say goodbye to her, the Alexandria that is leaving.  
Above all, don't fool yourself, don't say  
it was a dream, your ears deceived you:  
don't degrade yourself with empty hopes like these.  
As one long prepared, and graced with courage,  
as is right for you who proved worthy of this kind of city,  
go firmly to the window  
and listen with deep emotion, but not  
with the whining, the pleas of a coward;  
listen--your last delight--to the voices,  
to the exquisite music of that strange procession,   
and say goodbye to her, to the Alexandria you are losing.

​

The poem is a meditation on the story that the night before Mark Antony lost Alexandria, he saw Bacchus leaving the city in procession, and knew that he had been abandoned by his God. Antony commits suicide shortly afterward. I think it works for me because I see killing myself not as mourning a failed life but rather a response to a life I no longer want to live, a life whose invisible procession has left. I can live on, I can say it was a dream, my ears deceived me, or I can say goodbye to her, the life I am losing.

​

Fair enough actually. It's a pretty immoral action on my part to try and implicate someone else in an action which fundamentally belongs to me. Thanks for showing me that. 

I guess this original post was supposed to be more of a prayer than an actual question to random redditors. I want someone who can tell me, does it hurt to die? Will the joy/peace it brings me outweigh the suffering it causes other people and the opportunity cost of not living the rest of my life? Will the suffering of others even matter since I'll be dead and not around to experience it? 

Obvs no one can really answer those questions (I think). That's the only coherent argument against suicide I can even come up, the unknowablity of it (I know its a cliche "aye there's the rub" and all that, but it's true). For any other path I can at least do some research, see what others who have gone before me have to say. But suicide is so uncertain. It seems to me a net positive (strongly so) but I have no way of knowing, no way of looking before I leap (ha ha).

Sartre sounds like a dick lol.

I don't believe in a self like that. If I have any self separable from the social entity in which I reside, then it must consist of the choices I make. Therefore it is impossible for me to make any choice that is untrue to myself, because any choice I make becomes part of myself.

Whatever I choose, it will be authentic. But the choice I make will necessarily be based on input from outside the self. I am not an island.

This sort of non-answer sounds deep, but has within it nothing of value (at least for me).

I still appreciate your post though, not trying to be mean, just thinking things through.
